newsitem.title: FRANCE: French state bank says more state aid only way out.
newsitem.headline: French state bank says more state aid only way out.

text.p: The boss of Credit Lyonnais told French taxpayers Friday their lone hope of recouping some of the billions of francs of public money shovelled into the state-owned bank was by pumping in more and privatising it.

"It's in the taxpayers' interest and in the state's interest to privatise the bank in the best way possible, at the best price possible, to erase part of the bill," Jean Peyrelevade, chairman of Credit Lyonnais, said in a radio interview.

A day earlier the French had learned that the bank, whose plight ranks as France's worst banking horror story, needed to raid their wallets yet again -- this time to be recapitalized to prepare it for privatisation.

One newspaper, Liberation -- under the front-page banner headline "Should This Bank Be Saved?" -- estimated Friday that the ultimate bill to taxpayers from the bank's reckless expansion spree during the 1980s could hit 150 billion francs ($29 billion).

The bank, announcing a modest 67 million franc ($12.9 million) first-half profit, said late Thursday its balance sheet would need an injection of at least 8-9 billion francs ($1.54-1.74 billion) to attract a buyer and achieve the government's goal of rapid privatisation.

That recapitalization would be on top of 3.9 billion francs ($753 million) of emergency state aid announced last week to repair what turned out to be overly harsh terms of a state salvage last year that would have driven the bank back into the red.

The bank's warning that it would need to be recapitalized was not a big surprise. In announcing last week's aid, the government accelerated the privatisation timetable from the year 2000 and said the bank would need another full-scale bailout -- the third in the three years -- to prepare it for sale.

The government has not said how much it would pump into the bank, once the world's biggest outside Japan, but the press has been speculating on at least 10 billion francs ($1.9 billion), close to the amount the bank says may be needed.

The latest sums, however, are small when compared with losses of at least 90 billion francs ($17.4 billion) expected on the sale of the bank's dud assets amassed during its expansion binge and now housed in a separate, so-called "bad bank."
Credit Lyonnais, once France's flagship bank, rocketed in size during the late 1980s, then came crashing to earth in the early 1990s when property values collapsed and economic growth evaporated.
The bank eked out a 13 million franc ($ 2.5 million) profit in 1995 after racking up 21 billion francs ($4 billion) in losses between 1992 and 1994.
